findings.title: Cayman CRS Compliance Form deadline September 15, 2026 — 8 days away
findings.summary: For the 2025 reporting year, the Cayman Islands CRS Compliance Form is due September 15, 2026. The underlying CRS Return was due July 31, 2026. With 100+ partner jurisdictions now receiving full 2025 account data, non-compliance is highly detectable.
findings.client_impact: Any Cayman fund, SPV, or trust structure that has not yet filed its CRS Compliance Form must do so within 8 days or face CIMA enforcement. Clients with Cayman structures holding financial accounts for non-Cayman tax residents need to confirm filing status immediately.
findings.urgency_reason: Hard statutory deadline September 15, 2026 — 8 days from today. Failure to file risks CIMA penalties and reputational exposure to partner-jurisdiction tax authorities.

findings.title: CIMA AML/CFT/CPF Rule and Financial Sanctions Rule — compliance required by September 18, 2026
findings.summary: Two CIMA Rules carrying the force of law take effect September 18, 2026, imposing new mandatory AML audit cycles, enhanced outsourcing oversight, real-time sanctions screening, governance designations (AMLCO, MLRO, DMLRO), and fund-level risk assessments on all CIMA-registered entities including private and mutual funds.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients invested in or served by Cayman-registered funds must confirm that their fund administrator or manager has completed all required compliance steps — including governance appointments and independent AML audits — before September 18. Non-compliant funds risk CIMA enforcement action that could disrupt redemptions or fund operations.
findings.urgency_reason: Hard CIMA Rule effective date is September 18, 2026 — 11 days from today. All compliance infrastructure must be in place before that date; remediation windows close immediately.

findings.title: Belgium GIR notification deadline extended to September 30, 2026 — 23 days away
findings.summary: Belgium extended its GloBE Information Return notification form deadline for FY2024 from June 30, 2026 to September 30, 2026. The US formally exempted itself from Pillar Two. Over 60 jurisdictions are implementing GloBE rules as of mid-2026; the first OECD GIR filing deadline for calendar-year taxpayers was June 30, 2026 in most jurisdictions.
findings.client_impact: HNW clients who are part of multinational enterprise groups with Belgian entities and consolidated revenue ≥€750M must file their GIR notification with Belgian tax authorities by September 30, 2026. Missing this deadline exposes the group to administrative penalties and audit scrutiny in Belgium.
findings.urgency_reason: Belgium's GIR notification deadline is September 30, 2026 — 23 days from today. This is a hard administrative deadline; the prior June 30 date has already passed, making the September 30 extension the final opportunity to file without penalty.
findings.source_name: OECDPillars.com / PwC Pillar Two Country Tracker

findings.title: BCB VASP authorization deadline October 30, 2026 for grandfathered crypto firms
findings.summary: Brazil's BCB VASP (SPSAV) licensing regime entered force February 2, 2026. Pre-existing crypto platforms have until October 30, 2026 to apply for formal BCB authorization or face enforcement. Authorization requires substantial capital (R$10.8M–R$37.2M) and full AML/CFT compliance.
findings.client_impact: Clients invested in Brazilian crypto platforms or exchanges — or who use such platforms for digital-asset transactions — should verify their platform has applied for BCB authorization before October 30, as unauthorized platforms will face enforcement that could disrupt access to funds. Clients considering investments in Brazilian VASPs should factor licensing status into due diligence.
findings.urgency_reason: Deadline is October 30, 2026 — 53 days away. Classified WATCH rather than URGENT because this obligation falls on VASP operators, not wealth management clients directly; however, clients with exposure to Brazilian crypto platforms need to monitor their platforms' authorization status now.

findings.title: Cyprus Pillar Two amendments advancing after public consultation closed September 5, 2026
findings.summary: Cyprus closed a public consultation on July 30 – September 5, 2026 on amendments to align its Global Minimum Tax Law with OECD guidance and EC observations. Amendments expected to pass in autumn 2026. EU Commission confirmed qualified status of Cyprus's Income Inclusion Rule and safe harbors.
findings.client_impact: Clients using Cyprus holding or operating companies within MNE groups with revenue ≥€750M should track the forthcoming legislative amendments closely; changes to safe harbor availability or transition rules could affect effective tax rates and compliance obligations for Cyprus-based entities from FY2025 onwards.
findings.urgency_reason: No immediate deadline, but the autumn 2026 legislative timeline means rule changes are imminent. Clients with Cyprus structures in Pillar Two scope should engage local advisors now to model the impact of the amended rules before year-end.

findings.title: MAS August 2026 package: performance fee tax exemption, Hedge Fund Investment Programme, ONE Pass track for fund managers
findings.summary: MAS announced August 19, 2026 a three-part measure: (1) new tax exemption for performance/carry fees on qualifying funds from YA2027; (2) MAS will co-invest with hedge funds establishing Singapore presence; (3) new Investment Management Track under ONE Pass for talent visas. Singapore competes directly with London and Hong Kong for fund domicile.
findings.client_impact: Fund managers currently domiciled in or considering Singapore should evaluate whether the performance fee tax exemption (from YA2027) and MAS co-investment program make Singapore structuring materially more attractive; clients invested in funds considering a Singapore domicile shift may see fee economics and manager quality improve as a result.
findings.urgency_reason: No immediate client deadline, but the YA2027 effective date for the tax exemption means structuring decisions made in 2026 will determine eligibility. Managers and investors should begin preliminary analysis now.

findings.title: Luxembourg Pillar Two GIR filing operational; first international GIR data exchanges December 31, 2026
findings.summary: Luxembourg transposed DAC9 in December 2025; GIR filings for calendar-year entities were due June 30, 2026 via MyGuichet.lu. The first exchange of GIR data with partner jurisdictions will occur December 31, 2026. Luxembourg also introduced a 20% tax credit for qualifying investments in young innovative companies and increased pension savings deductions.
findings.client_impact: Clients with Luxembourg fund or holding structures within in-scope MNE groups must ensure their GIR was filed by June 30, 2026; if missed, remediation should begin immediately before the December exchange exposes gaps to foreign tax authorities. The new young-company investment credit may benefit clients with Luxembourg-based venture portfolios.
findings.urgency_reason: The June 30, 2026 GIR filing deadline has passed; the December 31 exchange date means any deficiency will become visible to partner-jurisdiction tax authorities in Q1 2027. Classified WATCH because no new deadline is imminent today, but unresolved filings carry growing risk.

findings.title: Guernsey private trust companies must now obtain fiduciary licence or limited permission; remediation required for existing PTCs
findings.summary: Guernsey's legislature passed trust law amendments on May 20, 2026, clarifying statutory provisions. The GFSC separately requires all PTCs — previously exempt — to obtain a full fiduciary licence or limited permission under the Fiduciaries Law. Existing PTCs must remediate; new PTCs must comply immediately. PTCs must operate within a licensed fiduciary's AML controls.
findings.client_impact: HNW families with Guernsey-based private trust companies must verify their PTC is either licensed or operating under a qualifying limited permission; failure to remediate exposes both the PTC and its administered trusts to regulatory action that could destabilise beneficiary arrangements or restrict trustee activity.
findings.urgency_reason: The GFSC requirement was issued in September 2025 for new PTCs and mandates remediation for existing ones on a timeline not publicly specified in available guidance. Classified WATCH because the deadline is not precisely known, but the obligation is current and non-compliance risk is live.

findings.title: Switzerland extends CRS 2.0 / CARF to crypto-assets effective January 2026; first crypto data exchanged from 2027
findings.summary: Switzerland's CRS 2.0 and CARF implementation took effect January 2026, requiring Swiss financial institutions and crypto platforms to report qualifying crypto holdings for automatic exchange with partner jurisdictions. Canton-level wealth tax on crypto continues. Cross-border salary data exchange with France and Italy begins 2027.
findings.client_impact: Clients with Swiss accounts or Swiss-based crypto platform accounts holding digital assets should assume those holdings are now subject to reporting to their home jurisdiction's tax authority; clients who have not previously disclosed Swiss crypto holdings face material tax and penalty risk and should seek voluntary disclosure advice promptly.
findings.urgency_reason: The reporting obligation is live from January 2026, but first data exchanges to partner jurisdictions will occur in 2027. The window for voluntary disclosure before foreign tax authorities receive data is narrowing, making this an active planning issue for non-compliant clients.

findings.title: UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 AML/CFT/CPF framework fully operational; enforcement stepped up in 2026
findings.summary: Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 (71 articles, ~300 requirements) established the UAE's most comprehensive AML/CFT framework. Mandatory goAML registration and a digital KYC platform are in force. UAE authorities increased inspections in 2026; DFSA's regulated population grew 14%, including a 75% increase in wealth management licences.
findings.client_impact: Clients with UAE wealth management, investment, or business accounts should expect more rigorous KYC refresh requests and transaction monitoring from their UAE-regulated service providers; clients with unreported beneficial ownership or opaque structures face heightened scrutiny as DFSA and other authorities expand enforcement.
findings.urgency_reason: No single filing deadline, but enforcement activity in 2026 is materially higher. Classified WATCH because clients with UAE exposure should proactively review their KYC documentation and structure disclosures with UAE advisors before an inspection or account review is triggered.

findings.title: MAS proposes ban on interest payments on MAS-regulated stablecoins; consultation open from September 1, 2026
findings.summary: MAS published a consultation on September 1, 2026 proposing to prohibit interest payments on MAS-regulated stablecoins, require 100% high-quality liquid reserve backing, and restrict use of the 'MAS-regulated' label to licensed issuers only. Follows Singapore's 2024 stablecoin licensing framework.
findings.client_impact: Clients holding MAS-regulated stablecoins as part of a yield strategy should be aware that interest payments may be prohibited, eliminating a key return source; wealth managers advising on digital-asset allocations should monitor the consultation outcome before recommending Singapore-regulated stablecoin positions.
findings.urgency_reason: Consultation is open; no implementation deadline specified yet. Classified WATCH because the prohibition, if enacted, would directly affect client return models for stablecoin-based strategies and requires portfolio review before the rule is finalised.

findings.title: CRS 2.0 and DAC8 (EU) effective January 2026: crypto-assets now subject to automatic information exchange globally
findings.summary: CRS 2.0 and EU DAC8 took effect January 2026, extending automatic information exchange to crypto-assets and aligning with the OECD Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). Financial institutions and crypto-asset service providers in CRS/DAC8 jurisdictions must collect and report client crypto holdings for cross-border exchange.
findings.client_impact: Clients holding crypto assets through financial institutions or crypto service providers in CRS/DAC8 jurisdictions should assume those holdings are now being captured for automatic exchange; clients who have not disclosed crypto assets in their home jurisdiction tax returns face increasing detection risk as the first data exchanges propagate through 2026–2027.
findings.urgency_reason: The reporting obligation is live from January 2026 with first exchanges occurring across 2026–2027. Classified WATCH as the window for voluntary disclosure narrows; clients with undisclosed crypto in CRS jurisdictions should engage tax counsel before the next filing season.

findings.title: FinCEN final rule effective August 14, 2026: all U.S.-formed entities permanently exempt from BOI reporting
findings.summary: FinCEN's August 14, 2026 final rule permanently removes BOI reporting requirements for all domestic U.S.-formed entities and their beneficial owners under the Corporate Transparency Act. Only foreign-formed entities registered to do business in the U.S. remain as reporting companies. FinCEN will delete previously submitted BOI from U.S. persons.
findings.client_impact: U.S.-domiciled clients with U.S.-formed LLCs, corporations, or partnerships no longer need to file or maintain BOI reports with FinCEN, eliminating a compliance burden and privacy concern. Clients with foreign-formed entities operating in the U.S. must still comply and should confirm their filing status.
findings.urgency_reason: Rule is already in effect as of August 14, 2026. No immediate client action required for domestic entities; the change is positive (obligation removed). Foreign-entity clients should have already filed; no new deadline arises from this rule.

findings.title: OBBBA permanently raises US estate/gift/GST exemption to $15M per person; prior sunset cliff eliminated
findings.summary: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently raised the per-person estate, gift, and GST exemption to $15M ($30M per married couple with portability), indexed for inflation from 2027. Annual gift exclusion remains $19,000. The prior 2025 sunset cliff — a major planning urgency — is eliminated. The act also caps itemized deductions at 35% for top-bracket taxpayers.
findings.client_impact: U.S. clients who completed estate planning under time pressure before the prior 2025 sunset can now reassess their structures at a calmer pace; clients who deferred planning can act without urgency at the $15M threshold. The itemized deduction cap may reduce the after-tax benefit of investment management fees for high-income clients.
findings.urgency_reason: Effective January 1, 2026 — already enacted. No immediate action required; the change removes prior urgency. Classified FYI as background awareness and a prompt to revisit existing estate plans that were structured around the old sunset assumptions.

findings.title: Trusts (Jersey) Amendment Law 2026 in force since March 20, 2026: sole-trustee resignation, Saunders v Vautier, lender priority
findings.summary: The 8th amendment to the Trusts (Jersey) Law 1984 came into force March 20, 2026: sole trustees cannot resign without appointing a successor; Saunders v Vautier does not apply where a power to add beneficiaries exists; lenders' secured interests take priority over trustee liens unless otherwise agreed.
findings.client_impact: Clients with Jersey trusts should be aware that beneficiaries can no longer compel termination of a trust with an add-beneficiary power, strengthening settlor intent protection; lenders financing against Jersey trust assets now have improved security priority, potentially enabling better financing terms for trust-held assets.
findings.urgency_reason: Already in force since March 20, 2026. No immediate action required. Classified FYI as background awareness; advisors should note the changed rules when reviewing existing Jersey trust deeds and advising on new structures.

findings.title: BVI statutory beneficial ownership registry open to legitimate-interest access since April 1, 2026; 25% threshold applies
findings.summary: From April 1, 2026, the BVI Financial Services Commission accepts applications from persons with legitimate interest to access the statutory beneficial ownership registry at a 25% ownership/control threshold. Entities that missed the January 1, 2026 filing deadline were marked 'In Penalty'; a moratorium ran until March 31, 2026.
findings.client_impact: Clients with BVI entities should confirm their beneficial ownership information is filed and current in the statutory registry, as third parties with legitimate interest (including regulators and law enforcement) can now access this data; the privacy landscape for BVI structures has materially changed from the legacy BOSS system.
findings.urgency_reason: Regime already live since April 1, 2026. No immediate filing deadline. Classified FYI because the key deadlines have passed; however, clients with non-compliant entities remain at risk of continuing penalties and should remediate without delay.

findings.title: Panama SBP Rule 1-2026 mandates enhanced AML documentation for bank onboarding of business clients
findings.summary: Panama's SBP Rule 1-2026 requires banks to collect a structured documentary pack — including a beneficial-ownership declaration to the ultimate natural person and an AML policy manual — before onboarding any business client. Draft Law 314 would introduce a fintech/crypto licensing regime. Panama was removed from the FATF grey list in 2023 and the EU high-risk list in 2025.
findings.client_impact: Clients opening or maintaining Panama corporate bank accounts should expect enhanced KYC documentation requests aligned with SBP Rule 1-2026, including disclosure of ultimate beneficial owners; clients who have not already provided this documentation may face account reviews or onboarding delays.
findings.urgency_reason: Rule already in force. No new deadline. Classified FYI as background awareness; advisors working on Panama entity onboarding should ensure documentary packs are prepared in advance of bank requests.

findings.title: Cyprus 8% flat crypto tax (Article 20E) and 15% corporate income tax effective January 1, 2026
findings.summary: From January 1, 2026, Cyprus applies an 8% flat tax on all crypto-asset disposals and income under Article 20E of the Income Tax Law, replacing previously ambiguous treatment. Corporate income tax rose from 12.5% to 15% to comply with EU Pillar Two minimum rate. Cyprus retains zero capital gains tax (except Cyprus real estate), no wealth, inheritance, or gift tax.
findings.client_impact: Clients holding crypto assets through Cyprus structures should factor the new 8% flat rate into their tax modeling for 2026 disposals; while 8% may still be competitive internationally, it replaces what was previously a more uncertain (often zero) treatment. The CIT increase to 15% slightly erodes Cyprus's corporate attractiveness for Pillar Two-exempt groups but the overall tax profile remains favorable.
findings.urgency_reason: Both changes effective January 1, 2026 — already in force. No immediate action. Classified FYI as background awareness for clients with Cyprus crypto exposure or corporate structures needing updated tax modeling.

findings.title: Florida SB 264 foreign real estate restrictions upheld by 11th Circuit; FIRPTA 15% withholding unchanged
findings.summary: The 11th Circuit upheld Florida SB 264 in November 2025, confirming restrictions on real estate purchases by nationals of seven designated countries (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, Venezuela, Syria). Chinese nationals face near-total ban near military/critical infrastructure. Affidavit requirement and forfeiture/criminal penalties remain. FIRPTA withholding stays at 15%. No new 2026 Florida legislation affecting foreign buyers.
findings.client_impact: Non-US clients from designated countries — particularly Chinese nationals — remain effectively barred from Florida real property acquisition and should continue to seek alternative U.S. real estate markets; all foreign buyers must continue to sign compliance affidavits and budget for 15% FIRPTA withholding on eventual sale proceeds.
findings.urgency_reason: Status quo confirmed. No new legislative change or deadline in 2026. Classified FYI as background confirmation that the existing framework remains intact; advisors should continue to screen client nationality against the designated-country list before any Florida real estate transaction.
